Modern.tagline: Souvenirs of the original cultural tourism.
Modern.brandNameRationale: The Grand Tour (1660s–1840s) was the European aristocratic coming-of-age circuit that established Western collecting — Roman bronzes, Venetian glass, Florentine intarsia. The phrase is public-domain art-historical vocabulary; 'Trade' names the dealer posture.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern antiques has split between fairs and online platforms. The opening is for a dealer who anchors on the Grand-Tour provenance category — small, documented objects with the original collecting context.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Galerie Steinitz (steinitz.fr) holds the Grand-Tour peer slot. Tomasso Brothers (tomassobrothers.co.uk) is the antiquities peer. Robilant + Voena (robilantvoena.com) plays the European decorative peer. We sit smaller than these, focused on documented Grand-Tour-provenance objects.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern antiques dealer in documented Grand-Tour-provenance objects.

targetAudience.primary: 45 to 70. Multi-generational collector. Furnishes a country house. Pays a premium for provenance.
behaviors: Buys at TEFAF and Frieze Masters

dos: Speak in object names, not styles

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Grand Tour Trade in a calm modern serif with a small itinerary-map mark above. The mark sits on certificates and the printed catalogue.

typography.primary: GT Sectra for the wordmark and catalogue
typography.secondary: Adobe Garamond for body and condition reports
typography.rationale: Sectra carries the scholarly register. Garamond keeps the long-form copy warm.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: The Society of Antiquaries of London was founded in 1707 and chartered in 1751 — the oldest learned society for the study of the past. The phrase 'Antiquarian Society' is the public-domain category name, not the institution's mark; it signals society-level scholarship.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury antiques is dominated by the big three auction houses. The opening is for a small house with documented society-level cataloguing — every lot researched by a fellow, every provenance documented.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Sotheby's (sothebys.com) is the global benchmark. Christie's (christies.com) holds the institutional-luxury slot. Mallett (mallettantiques.com) plays the heritage-decorative peer position. We sit smaller and more scholarly than these.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A luxury antiques house with society-level scholarship on every lot.

targetAudience.primary: 50 to 80. Multi-generational collector. Donates to museums. Requires documented provenance.
behaviors: Pays a premium for documented provenance

dos: Cite the fellow who catalogued the lot

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Antiquarian Society set in a classical English roman with a small society-seal mark above (a stylized antiquarian's lens). The mark appears on the catalogue cover and every lot certificate.

typography.primary: Caslon for the wordmark and catalogue
typography.secondary: Adobe Garamond for condition reports and correspondence
typography.rationale: Caslon carries 250 years of British scholarly printing. Garamond handles the longer-form copy.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Patina — the surface layer (oxidized bronze, waxed wood, worn silver) — authenticates age in the antiques trade. The brand sits on the single most important word in dealer vocabulary, and treats it as a non-negotiable: surface only, untouched, never restored.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal antiques is an oxymoron in a category obsessed with provenance stories. The opening is for a dealer who strips the narrative and sells purely on surface: patina-only, no restoration, no story.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: BDDW (bddw.com) holds the minimal-considered-design slot translated to antiques. Drag-On Antiques (no peer URL) sits in the minimal-antiquarian position. The Future Perfect (thefutureperfect.com) plays the considered-modern peer reference. We sit further out — surface-only, untouched.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Minimal antiques. Surface only. Never restored.

targetAudience.primary: 35 to 60. Owns one home, furnishes slowly. Cares about surface integrity over completeness. Reads the patina before the receipt.
behaviors: Buys one piece every two years

dos: Show the surface in raking light

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark — Patina Co. in a humanist sans with a small patina-swatch icon (a soft oxidized circle) above. The icon alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: ABC Diatype for the wordmark and body
typography.secondary: ABC Diatype Mono for condition reports
typography.rationale: One family. Mono for the wear data.

Corporate.tagline: Title-grade provenance research and due diligence.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Provenance — the chain-of-ownership record — is the single most valuable attribute in the antiques and fine-art trade, especially post-Washington Principles (1998) and post-restitution legislation. The phrase names the firm's only product: title-grade research.
Corporate.industrySummary: Corporate antiques is a serious B2B category — provenance research, restitution review, title insurance. Institutional collectors, museum acquisition committees, and estate executors need due-diligence-grade documentation, not retail catalogues.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Art Loss Register (artloss.com) holds the registry-and-research slot. ArtIndex (no peer URL) sits in the provenance-research position. Constance Lowenthal Associates (no peer URL) plays the restitution-research peer. We sit between these as a multi-service provenance firm.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Corporate provenance research and title due diligence for institutional collectors.

targetAudience.primary: 45 to 65. Museum acquisition committees, institutional collectors, estate executors, title-insurance underwriters.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small chain-link mark — PROVENANCE GROUP set in a tight grotesk above a single linked-chain icon. Reads cleanly on title-insurance documents, museum reports, and trade-show banners.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and B2B materials
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed research reports and contracts
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles printed due-diligence documentation.

Creative.tagline: Empty the attic. No two visits the same.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Vide-grenier ('empty the attic') is the French neighborhood flea-market tradition codified in the 1970s. The phrase is public-domain French vernacular; it names the rotating-stock posture of a small creative shop.
Creative.industrySummary: Creative antiques is crowded with curated 'vintage' shops. The opening is for a French-flea-market-style dealer with no fixed catalogue — rotating stock, no online inventory, no two visits alike.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen (marcheauxpuces-saintouen.com) is the institutional flea-market reference. Cabana Magazine (cabanamagazine.com) holds the creative-eclectic peer slot. Casa Lopez (casalopez.com) plays the Parisian-creative peer position. We sit closer to Casa Lopez in scope with a sharper rotating-stock identity.
Creative.positioningStatement: A French-flea-market-style creative antiques dealer with rotating stock and no fixed catalogue.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Renters or first-home owners. Visit the shop in person. Buy on the day, not from a website.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — Vide-Grenier set in a friendly French sans with a small hand-drawn attic-door icon above. The icon appears on stickers and shop bags.

typography.primary: PP Mori for the wordmark and headlines
typography.rationale: Mori carries the friendly French shop register. Sectra makes the object descriptions feel like a small magazine.
